subject: chemistry
question_text: Explain the different types of intermolecular forces.

mark_split.label: Hydrogen bonding and the strength order

verification.note: PREDICTED, not asked. This card comes from the Chapter 4 enumeration sweep: intermolecular forces open the NCERT States of Matter chapter, yet the Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.62-66) skips the whole topic — an entire syllabus section with no question. Only ONE chemistry source book is held, so the two-book union check is PENDING. The book prints NO Long Answer section for this chapter, so no 8-mark form is invented. The mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. AI chemistry check 2026-08-25. The three forces described are correct and the strength order dispersion < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bond is right, but the card omits NCERT's FOURTH type — dipole–induced dipole (Debye) forces — on a question that asks for the different types. The mark split is fixed at three steps, so the omission is recorded in the dipole–dipole step's margin_note rather than added as a step; a teacher must decide whether the 4-mark answer has to name all four. No marked line changed. AI chemistry check 2026-08-25 (audit round 3), two items. (1) The step-2 note told the student to add the fourth type if the question asks for ALL the types, but this card's own question asks for the different types, so that condition may already be met while the mark split funds only three; the note now states plainly that the three funded types are the answer and the fourth is background. OPEN FOR THE TEACHER GATE: whether a 4-mark answer must name dipole–induced dipole as a fourth type, and if so how the split changes. (2) The boxed strength order was stated unconditionally while the similar-size qualifier sat in a why the student never copies; the step-3 why now carries that qualifier. No marked line changed and no mark moved.

steps.label: Dispersion (London) forces
lines: between momentary dipoles, formed when the
electron cloud of a molecule is unevenly spread
They exist between ALL molecules, including
non-polar ones (H₂, N₂, noble gases), and grow
steps.why: Non-polar substances still liquefy, so some attraction must exist even without permanent dipoles. Momentary uneven electron distribution supplies it, which is why this force is universal.
common_mistakes: Saying non-polar molecules have no intermolecular forces at all. Dispersion forces act between every pair of molecules.
Calling the momentary dipole a permanent one.
steps.memory_tip: London forces are present in every substance, and they are the ONLY intermolecular force in non-polar ones.
steps.margin_note: Momentary (instantaneous) dipole is the marked phrase.

steps.label: Dipole–dipole forces
lines: permanent dipoles of polar molecules — the
positive end of one molecule attracts the
Example: HCl molecules in the liquid.
steps.why: A polar molecule carries a built-in charge separation, so neighbouring molecules line up positive-to-negative. The attraction is stronger than dispersion between molecules of similar size.
common_mistakes: Giving a non-polar example such as CO₂. The molecule must have a permanent dipole — HCl is the safe example.
Confusing this with the ion–ion attraction of salts, which is far stronger.
steps.memory_tip: Permanent plus-to-minus pairing — the polar molecules' own force.
steps.margin_note: One named polar example completes the point. NCERT names a fourth type between this one and hydrogen bonding — dipole–induced dipole (Debye) forces, where a polar molecule induces a dipole in a non-polar neighbour. The three types above are the answer this mark split pays for; the fourth is background, not a fourth marked point.

steps.label: Hydrogen bonding and the strength order
lines: attraction, formed when H is covalently bonded
to a small, highly electronegative atom — N, O
or F — and is attracted to the N, O or F of a

lines.text: Strength order: dispersion < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bond

steps.why: Bonding to N, O or F strips the small hydrogen atom of electron density, leaving an exposed positive centre that binds strongly to a neighbour's lone pair. That special case earns its own name and the top of the strength order. The order compares molecules of similar size: dispersion forces grow with molecular size, so between large non-polar molecules they can be stronger than the dipole–dipole forces between small polar ones. The boxed line is the board's answer and is written as it stands.
common_mistakes: Extending hydrogen bonding to H bonded to C or Cl. Only N, O and F qualify.
Calling the hydrogen bond a covalent bond. It is an intermolecular attraction, much weaker than a covalent bond.
steps.memory_tip: N, O, F — the only three atoms that give hydrogen bonding, and water is the standard example.
steps.margin_note: The boxed order line is the summarising mark; all three force names must appear above it.

insider_note: Three forces but four marks, because hydrogen bonding shares two of them with the strength order. Three good descriptions with no ranking line at the end leave half of that pair unearned.
